rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He suggests a coherence: after distinguishing believers’ fasting rules from earlier communities, the passage warns them against imitating scriptural communities’ bribes, usury, and unlawful wealth-taking.
rows.anchor: أنه لما أوجب عليهم الصوم، كما أوجبه على من كان من قبلهم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet urged opposition to Jews when encouraging the pre-dawn meal.
rows.anchor: لما ندب إلى السحور: «خالفوا اليهود»

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: When Companions isolated menstruating women in imitation of Jewish practice, he told them to do everything except intercourse; Jews then complained that he opposed all their customs.
rows.anchor: فقال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: «افعلوا كل شيء إلا النكاح»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Eating” most naturally means literal consumption, named because it meets the greatest need and destroys much property; it may also figuratively mean taking or appropriating wealth.
rows.anchor: والمفهوم من قوله تعالى: ولا تأكلوا، الأكل المعروف، لأنه الحقيقة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address is to believers: do not take one another’s wealth, just as “do not kill yourselves” means do not kill one another; the shared pronoun marks each person as both forbidden actor and victim, and forbids enabling another’s taking.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: ولا يأكل بعضكم مال بعض، كقوله: ولا تقتلوا أنفسكم

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some take the possessive literally for owners and explain unlawful wealth as entertainments, singing women, drinking, and misconduct in dealings and trusts.
rows.anchor: وأجاز قوم الإضافة للمالكين، وفسروا الباطل بالملاهي والقيان والشرب

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj glosses “falsehood” as wrongdoing; another explanation includes every unsanctioned means, such as usurpation, plunder, gambling, soothsayers’ fees, treachery, bribes, and astrologers’ earnings.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج بالظلم، وقال غيره بالجهة التي لا تكون مشروعة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the verse concerns a debtor who denies a debt despite having no proof against him, then litigates while knowing he sins.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: هذا في الرجل يكون عليه مال ولا بينة عليه

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima applies it to someone who buys an item, returns it, and also demands money with it.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: هو الرجل يشتري السلعة فيردها ويرد معها دراهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas also includes acquiring money through false testimony.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس، أيضا: هو أخذ المال بشهادة الزور

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya excludes deceptive price advantage when the seller knows what he sells, treating it as a gift; Abu Hayyan says this is correct.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: ولا يدخل فيه الغبن في البيع مع معرفة البائع بحقيقة ما يبيع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Between you” is metaphorical: a spatial expression is extended to people and their transactions; wrongdoing visible among participants is especially heinous, supporting the reading that the wealth is not literally each owner’s own.
rows.anchor: والبينية مجاز إذ موضوعها أنها ظرف مكان، ثم تجوز فيها فاستعملت في أشخاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Parsing “between you” as a circumstantial phrase modifying “your wealth,” with an implied “existing,” is weak.
rows.anchor: وقيل: انتصاب: بينكم، على الحال من: أموالكم، فيتعلق بمحذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition in “by falsehood” marks cause and attaches to “eat”; alternatively it may describe the wealth or the actor circumstantially.
rows.anchor: والباء في: بالباطل، للسبب وهي تتعلق: بتأكلوا، وجوزوا أن تكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “And do not deliver it” is coordinated with the prohibition; Ubayy’s codex explicitly repeats the negative particle. The pronoun means wealth, so both wrongful acquisition and using wealth to secure it are forbidden.
rows.anchor: وتدلوا بها إلى الحكام هو مجزوم بالعطف على النهي

rows.speaker: الأخفش وغيره
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash and others allow the accusative after the prohibition by supplying an implicit أن; al-Zamakhshari also allows it.
rows.anchor: وأجاز الأخفش وغيره أن يكون منصوبا على جواز النهي بإضمار أن

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya reports a Kufan parsing that makes “deliver” accusative through an adverbial operator; Sibawayh instead requires an implicit أن, and Abu Hayyan finds no decisive Arabic evidence for the Kufan rule.
rows.anchor: وحكى ابن عطية أنه قيل: تدلوا، في موضع نصب على الظرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative reading as a ban only on combining the two actions fails: forbidding the combination does not forbid each separately, while forbidding each entails forbidding their combination.
rows.anchor: إذا نصبت كان الكلام نهيا عن الجمع بينهما، وهذا المعنى لا يصح في الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stronger objection is causal: “so that you consume” explains the preceding prohibition, but a joint action cannot be its cause; only delivering wealth to judges does.
rows.anchor: أن قوله لتأكلوا علة لما قبلها، فلو كان النهي عن الجمع لم تصلح العلة له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation of delivering wealth is rushing into litigation when one knows the opponent lacks proof, or when the property is a trust whose possessor’s word is accepted; the preposition marks cause.
rows.anchor: والإدلاء هنا قيل: معناه الإسراع بالخصومة في الأموال إلى الحكام

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya prefers the bribery interpretation: judges are especially susceptible to bribes except for a rare protected few, and “deliver” and “bribe-rope” evoke lowering a bucket to obtain one’s need; Abu Hayyan agrees it is good.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وهذا القول يترجح، لأن الحاكم مظنة الرشاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further explanation is to incline toward judges with one’s plea; this returns to the litigation interpretation. A more remote reading makes the pronoun refer to false testimony, whether witnesses or beneficiaries are being forbidden.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المعنى لا تجنحوا بها إلى الحكام من قولهم: أدلى فلان بحجته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “A portion” means a piece or amount; although some specify orphans’ property or deposits, he prefers the general sense of any property wrongfully obtained through adjudication.
rows.anchor: والأولى العموم، وأن ذلك عبارة عن أخذ كل مال يتوصل إليه في الحكومة بغير حق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “By sin” has been explained as false testimony, bribery, false oath, or settling knowingly for the wrongdoer; Abu Hayyan prefers the inclusive rule that any sinful means of taking money is sin.
rows.anchor: وفسر بالحكم بشهادة الزور، وقيل: بالرشوة، وقيل: بالحلف الكاذب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root sense of sin is falling short or failing in a duty; it then names failure toward God and wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: والأصل في الإثم التقصير في الأمر قال الشاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition in “by sin” can mark cause or a state of being involved in wrongdoing; “while you know” is circumstantial and stresses knowingly violating others’ rights.
rows.anchor: والباء في: بالإثم للسبب، ويحتمل أن تكون للحال أي: متلبسين بالإثم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet warns that a person awarded another’s right must not take it, since the judgment awards only a piece of fire.
rows.anchor: فمن قضيت له بشيء من حق أخيه فلا يأخذ منه شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse and hadith forbid wrongfully taking others’ wealth; a court ruling does not make known unlawful property lawful. Scholars agree on property, but differ about contracts and dissolutions adjudicated on false testimony.
rows.anchor: وظاهر الحديث والآية تحريم ما أخذ من مال الناس بالإثم

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa holds a judge’s ruling in a contract or rescission effective inwardly as well as outwardly, even when based on false witnesses.
rows.anchor: فقال أبو حنيفة: هو نافذ، وهو كالإنشاء وإن كانوا شهود زور

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority hold such a ruling effective outwardly but not in the underlying reality.
rows.anchor: وقال الجمهور: ينفذ ظاهرا ولا ينفذ باطنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “while you know” implies that an unaware person may take what a judge awards: for example, a proven debt owed to one’s father, where payment or gift is possible but the presumption is that the debt remains due.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله: وأنتم تعلمون دلالة على أن من لم يعلم أنه آثم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage opens warmly to believers and presents fasting as a difficult duty shared with earlier communities to encourage emulation and hope for piety, then lightens it with a limited number of days and exemptions for illness and travel, requiring make-up days.
rows.anchor: وقد تضمنت هذه الآيات الكريمة نداء المؤمنين تقريبا لهم، وتحريكا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The initial law allowed an able faster who chose not to fast to feed poor people; voluntary good was praised and fasting was better than breaking the fast and paying compensation, before Ramadan fasting abrogated that rule.
rows.anchor: ثم ذكر أن التطوع بالخير، هو خير، وأن الصوم أفضل من الفطر، والفداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Legal obligations characteristically begin with what is easier and proceed to the required limit, where the ruling settles.
rows.anchor: وهكذا جرت العادة في التكاليف الشرعية يبتدأ فيها أولا بالأخف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The month’s virtue is tied to revelation of the Qur’an; residents must fast it, while the sick and traveler make up what they missed after recovery or settling, in keeping with divine intent to ease the burden.
rows.anchor: ونبه على فضيلة هذا الشهر المفروض بأنه الشهر الذي أنزل فيه الوحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prescribed month, exemption for illness and travel, and divine desire for ease serve completion of the count, magnification of God, and gratitude, each law being paired with its fitting purpose.
rows.anchor: ثم ذكر أن مشروعية صوم الشهر، وإباحة الفطر للمريض والمسافر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After worshippers glorify God, the passage stresses His nearness and response to supplication, asks them to answer His call, continue in faith, and thereby hope for right guidance.
rows.anchor: ثم لما ذكر تعالى تعظيم العباد لربهم والثناء عليه منهم، ذكر قربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After requiring faith as the foundation of sound worship, God permits marital intercourse on fasting nights because spouses are garments for one another; He pardons past violations, commands intimacy and eating and drinking until dawn, requires fasting until night, and forbids intercourse during mosque retreat.
rows.anchor: ثم امتن عليهم تعالى بإحلال ما كانوا ممنوعين منه، وهو النكاح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibitions are God’s boundaries; forbidding even approaching them intensifies the command to keep distant, and clear signs and legal proofs are explained in hope of piety.
rows.anchor: ثم أشار إلى الحواجز وهي: الحدود، وأضافها إليه ليعلم أن الذي حدها هو الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage forbids taking one another’s wealth by unsanctioned means and bribing corrupt judges to obtain what one is not owed; knowing violation aggravates blame because deliberate sin is more heinous than ignorant sin.
rows.anchor: ثم نهاهم عن أن يأكل بعضهم مال بعض بالباطل، وهي الطريق التي لم يبح الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage begins with the binding command to fast and concludes with a prohibition on unlawful wealth, so the fast is broken with lawful food and may be accepted, unlike a fast yielding only hunger and thirst.
rows.anchor: وكان من أعظم ممنوعاته وأكبرها الأكل فيه، اختتم هذه الآيات بالنهي

rows.speaker: حديث
rows.claim: A report instructs a fasting person who is insulted to say, “I am fasting.”
rows.anchor: في الحديث: «فإن امرئ سبه، فليقل:

rows.speaker: الله تعالى
rows.claim: A divine report says that fasting belongs to God and He Himself rewards it.
rows.anchor: وجاء عن الله تعالى: «الصوم لي وأنا أجزي به»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage frames duty with duty and prohibition: commands and bans run through the intervening verses, asking God to help believers observe both.
rows.anchor: فافتتحت هذه الآيات بواجب مأمور به، واختتمت بمحرم منهي عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Bahata” means to be bewildered or stunned; it may be transitive or intransitive, and related forms can mean confronting someone with a lie.
rows.anchor: بهت: تحير ودهش، ويكون متعديا على وزن فعل

rows.speaker: حديث
rows.claim: A hadith characterizes the Jews as a people prone to falsehood.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث إن اليهود قوم بهت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Khāwī” means empty; its related forms also refer to a collapsed house, hunger, a woman’s empty womb after childbirth, and food set aside for her.
rows.anchor: الخاوي: الخالي، خوت الدار تخوي خوى غير ممدود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Arsh” is a roof or any structure made for shade, such as a vine trellis; the Qur’an also uses the root for what people build.
rows.anchor: العرش: سقف البيت، وكل ما يهيأ ليظل أو يكن فهو عريش الدالية

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report about building the mosque says the Prophet wanted a simple palm-frond shelter like Moses’ shelter.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث لما أمر ببناء المسجد قالوا: نبنيه لك بنيانا قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited rajaz line uses “khawā” for a camel’s posture, with its belly raised above the ground while resting or prostrating.
rows.anchor: خوى على مستويات خمس ... كركرة وثفنات ملس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Arsh” can also mean a building, as illustrated by a poem about razing a people’s structures.
rows.anchor: إن يقتلوك فقد ثللث عروشهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “One hundred” is a known numerical rank, pluralized as hundreds; its weak final letter is omitted, its original form is mئة, and the verb means making or becoming one hundred.
rows.anchor: مائة: اسم لرتبة من العدد معروفة، ويجمع على مئات ومئين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A year is a known span; its alif derives from wāw, as shown by “years.”
rows.anchor: العام: مدة من الزمان معروفة، وألفه منقلبة عن واو

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash proposes that “year” is a verbal noun like swimming, named because the sun swims through its orbit; the cited Qur’anic phrase supports the swimming image.
rows.anchor: وقال النقاش: العام مصدر كالعوم، سمي به هذا القدر من الزمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Labth” means remaining or residing.
rows.anchor:
اللبث: المكث والإقامة.
يتسنه:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the hāʾ of “yatassannah” is original, the word derives from year; diminutive, plural, and Hijazi verb forms support that analysis.
rows.anchor: إن كانت الهاء أصلية فهو من السنة على من يجعل لامها المحذوف هاء

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad treats the final hāʾ as a pause marker; then the weak final letter is omitted under jussive mood and the word derives from year, with further proposed derivations from change or from altered “molded.”
rows.anchor: وإن كانت الهاء للسكت، وهو اختيار المبرد، فلام الكلمة محذوفة للجازم

rows.speaker: أبو عمر
rows.claim: Abu Umar derives the form from “masnūn” meaning changed, with sound changes avoiding repeated consonants; al-Zajjaj rejects this because “masnūn” means shaped on a path.
rows.anchor: قاله أبو عمر، وخطأه الزجاج. قال: لأن المسنون: المصبوب على سنة الطريق

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash derives “yatassannah” from water that has not become stale; grammarians object that the expected form would be “yata’assan.”
rows.anchor: وقال النقاش: هو من قوله من ماء غير آسن

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ali reads “alam tara” with a quiescent final rāʾ, applying pause pronunciation across a connection.
rows.anchor: وقرأ علي بن أبي طالب: ألم تر، بسكون الراء

rows.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة والربيع والسدي وابن إسحاق وزيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: These authorities identify the disputant as Nimrod son of Canaan son of Cush son of Shem, a ruler associated with the fire and the mosquito.
rows.anchor: قاله مجاهد، وقتادة، والربيع، والسدي، وابن إسحاق، وزيد بن أسلم

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says Nimrod was the first king on earth; Ibn Atiyya rejects that claim.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جريج: هو أول ملك في الأرض، ورده ابن عطية

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada calls Nimrod the first tyrant and owner of Babylon’s tower; another report says he ruled the entire world.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: هو أول من تجبر، وهو صاحب الصرح ببابل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid divides world-rulers into two believing kings, Solomon and Dhu al-Qarnayn, and two unbelieving kings, Nimrod and Nebuchadnezzar.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: ملك الأرض مؤمنان: سليمان وذو القرنين، وكافران: نمروذ

rows.speaker: السهيلي
rows.claim: Al-Suhayli gives a different lineage and associates Nimrod with the Sudanese king al-Dahhak, later killed by Afridun; Abu Tammam likens a patron to Afridun in a poem.
rows.anchor: وحكى السهيلي أنه: النمروذ بن كوش بن كنعان بن حام بن نوح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “He disputed with Abraham about his Lord” can mean he countered Abraham’s proof, brought a rebuttal, or sought to prevail in argument.
rows.anchor: ومعنى: حاج إبراهيم في ربه أي: عارض حجته بمثلها، أو: أتى على الحجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account places the debate after Abraham broke the idols during a festival; when asked whom he worshipped, he named the Lord who gives life and death.
rows.anchor: قيل: خرجوا إلى عيد لهم، فدخل إبراهيم على أصنامهم فكسرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other accounts place the dispute in Nimrod’s grain-rationing court: visitors prostrated to receive food, while Abraham refused and named his Lord; another says Nimrod routinely asked each visitor to acknowledge him as lord.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله: إنه كان كلما جاء قوم قال من ربكم وإلهكم؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further report says the debate followed Abraham’s escape from the fire: denied food, he carried sand home, where it became excellent food by God’s provision; a variant says red sand became red wheat.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كانت المحاجة بعد أن خرج من النار التي ألقاه فيها النمروذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “about his Lord” most naturally refers to Abraham, though it could refer to Nimrod.
rows.anchor: في: ربه، يحتمل أن يعود الضمير على إبراهيم، وأن يعود على النمروذ، والظاهر الأول.

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority take the pronoun in “when God gave him kingship” to refer to the disputant; the causal phrase means kingship made him arrogant, or that he challenged God instead of showing gratitude for it.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أن الضمير في: آتاه، عائد على: الذي حاج، وهو قول الجمهور

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari proposes a temporal reading, “at the time He gave him kingship”; Abu Hayyan finds it strained unless time means a broad period, and rejects treating the clause itself as a temporal noun.
rows.anchor: وأجاز الزمخشري أن يكون التقدير: حاج وقت أن آتاه الله الملك

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawi allows the pronoun to refer to Abraham, meaning God gave him the kingship of prophethood.
rows.anchor: وقال المهدوي: يحتمل أن يعود الضمير على إبراهيم: أي آتاه ملك النبوة.

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya calls al-Mahdawi’s interpretation an overstrained reading; the view that Abraham received kingship is associated with the Muʿtazila, who cite God’s covenant and the great kingdom given to Abraham’s family.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وهذا تحامل من التأويل. انتهى. وما ذكره المهدوي احتمالا هو قول المعتزلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects the proposed objections to Abraham’s kingship: spiritual authority as prophethood can coexist with Nimrod’s worldly power, wealth, and coercive rule.
rows.anchor: ولا يرد على المعتزلة بهذه الأوجه، لأن إثبات ملك النبوة لإبراهيم لا ينافي ملك الكافر

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Asked why God gives kingship to an unbeliever, al-Zamakhshari answers that worldly assets and followers were given, or that kingship tested people; Abu Hayyan detects Muʿtazilite doctrine in denying divine enabling of domination.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: فإن قلت: كيف جاز أن يؤتي الله الملك الكافر؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s statement that his Lord gives life and death answers the disputant’s prior question about who his Lord is; it would not begin an unprompted exchange.
rows.anchor: هذا من إبراهيم عن سؤال سبق من الكافر، وهو أن قال: من ربك؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham invokes life and death because they are among God’s most original, renowned signs of power; the “when” clause grammatically attaches to “disputed.”
rows.anchor: واختص إبراهيم من آيات الله بالإحياء والإماتة لأنهما أبدع آيات الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari’s proposal that the “when” clause substitutes for “when He gave him kingship” is weak because the two events occurred at different times; Abraham’s wording also supports taking “his Lord” as Abraham’s Lord.
rows.anchor: وقد ذكرنا ضعف ذلك، وأيضا فالظرفان مختلفان إذ وقت إيتاء الملك ليس وقت قوله

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says Abraham could have answered Nimrod by asking him to revive a killed man; one report says he did, then added the sun argument to end debate rather than from weakness.
rows.anchor: ومعنى قول الزمخشري: وكان الاعتراض عتيدا: أي من إبراهيم، لو أراد أن يعترض عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On one account Nimrod claimed divinity and pretended that killing one man and sparing another meant he gave life and death; Abraham then challenged him to bring the sun from the west, exposing his inability.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كان نمروذ يدعي الربوبية، فلما قال له: إبراهيم ربي الذي يحيي ويميت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says Nimrod challenged Abraham to prove he had seen resurrection; Abraham moved to a clearer sign visible to both men.
rows.anchor: وقيل: لما قال: ربي الذي يحيي ويميت قال له النمروذ: وأنت رأيت هذا؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further explanation says Abraham chose the sun because his interlocutors revered it, showing that it too was subject to God.
rows.anchor: كانوا يعظمون الشمس، فأشار إلى أنها لله عز وجل مقهورة

rows.speaker: المحققون
rows.claim: The conjunction implies an omitted conditional challenge; Abu Hayyan reconstructs it as Abraham saying that if Nimrod claimed such power, God brings the sun as described.
rows.anchor: وتقدير الجملة، والله أعلم قال إبراهيم إن زعمت ذلك أو موهت بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conjunction in “for God brings the sun” implies an omitted prior conditional thought, such as “if you claim that, then God brings the sun”; the preposition makes the sun the object moved, and مِن marks origin.
rows.anchor: ومجيء الفاء في: فإن، يدل على جملة محذوفة قبلها، إذ لو كانت هي المحكية فقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most reciters read “fa-buhita” passively; its omitted agent is Abraham or his utterance. Other readings are active: Ibn al-Sumayfiʿ may mean Abraham stunned the unbeliever, the unbeliever insulted Abraham, or the unbeliever uttered falsehood; Abu Haywa and a reading reported by al-Akhfash vary the vowel.
rows.anchor: فبهت الذي كفر قراءة الجمهور مبنيا لما لم يسم فاعله

rows.speaker: ابن السميفع
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sumayfiʿ reads the verb actively with fatḥa on both letters; interpretations include Abraham stunning the unbeliever, the defeated unbeliever insulting Abraham, or the unbeliever speaking falsely.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن السميفع: فبهت، بفتح الباء والهاء

rows.speaker: أبو حيوة
rows.claim: Abu Haywa reads the verb with fatḥa on bāʾ and ḍamma on hāʾ; al-Akhfash also reports a kasra reading.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو حيوة: فبهت، بفتح الباء وضم الهاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “God does not guide the unjust” has been restricted to guidance in argument, entry to reward or Paradise, or divine inspiration and enabling; some restrict “unjust” to those who die as unbelievers.
rows.anchor: فما ذكر في الهداية الخاصة أنه لا يرشدهم في حجتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan takes the statement to concern those decreed to persist as unbelievers, who cannot receive guidance; the claim to divine power is blatant injustice, and God leaves Nimrod stunned to honor Abraham and manifest the truth.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر أن هذا إخبار من الله بأن من حكم عليه، وقضى بأن يكون ظالما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says Nimrod did not claim to control sunrise because his subjects knew the sun preceded him, nor sunset because he knew he could not do it; he fell silent.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنما لم يدع أنه هو الذي يأتي بها من المشرق، لظهور كذبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read “aw” with a still wāw and explain it as either differentiation or a choice that heightens wonder at the two examples.
rows.anchor: قرأ الجمهور: أو، ساكنة الواو، قيل: ومعناها التفصيل

rows.speaker: أبو سفيان بن حسين
rows.claim: Abu Sufyan ibn Husayn reads the wāw open, with an interrogative hamza understood: “Did you see the like of the one who passed?”
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو سفيان بن حسين: أو كالذي، بفتح الواو

rows.speaker: جمهور المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes coordinate the second example by meaning with the first, since “Have you not seen?” means “Have you seen?”; Arabic permits such coordination by sense, though it is not analogically productive.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ: أو، بحرف العطف فجمهور المفسرين أنه معطوف على قوله: ألم تر إلى الذي حاج

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari supplies an omitted “did you see the like of” from the preceding expression of wonder; Abu Hayyan prefers this straightforward ellipsis to coordination by sense.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري، أو كالذي: معناه أو رأيت مثل الذي؟ فحذف لدلالة: ألم تر؟ عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some call the kāf redundant so that “the one” coordinates directly with the earlier “one”; another analysis treats kāf as a noun governed by the preposition, a recognized but remote use.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الكاف زائدة، فيكون: الذي، قد عطف على: الذي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan finds the nominal kāf analysis linguistically possible but remote; he judges the omitted-verb explanation preferable and notes that coordination by sense is not analogical.
rows.anchor: وتأويلها بعيد، فالأولى هذا الوجه الأخير، وإنما عرض لهم الإشكال

rows.speaker: علي وابن عباس وعكرمة وأبو العالية وسعيد بن جبير وقتادة والربيع والضحاك والسدي ومقاتل
rows.claim: These authorities identify the passerby as Uzayr.
rows.anchor: قاله علي، وابن عباس، وعكرمة، وأبو العالية، وسعيد بن جبير، وقتادة

rows.speaker: وهب ومجاهد وعبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير وبكر بن مضر
rows.claim: These authorities identify the passerby as Jeremiah; Ibn Ishaq calls him Jeremiah who is al-Khidr, as transmitted from Wahb by al-Naqqash.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أرمياء، قاله وهب، ومجاهد، وعبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير، وبكر

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya rejects identifying the passerby with al-Khidr because Khidr was Moses’ contemporary whereas this man lived later, though one of his teachers allows Khidr as a long-lived survivor.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وهذا كما نراه إلا أن يكون اسما وافق اسما

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says the passerby was an unnamed unbeliever riding a donkey and carrying a basket of figs; other reports name an Israelite, Lot’s servant, or Shuʿyaʾ.
rows.anchor: وقيل: على كافر مر على قرية وكان على حمار ومعه سلة تين، قاله الحسن

rows.speaker: السهيلي
rows.claim: Al-Suhayli, citing al-Qutaybi, says the one who revived the city was the Persian Lusak.
rows.anchor: والذي أحياها بعد خرابها: لوسك الفارسي، حكاه السهيلي عن القتيبي

rows.speaker: وهب وقتادة والضحاك وعكرمة والربيع
rows.claim: These authorities identify the city as Jerusalem; other locations proposed are a nearby grape village, the Holy Land, al-Muʾtafikah, the village from which people fled death, Heraclius’ monastery, Shabur Abad, and Salmayadh.
rows.anchor: والقرية: بيت المقدس، قاله وهب، وقتادة، والضحاك، وعكرمة، والربيع

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says the village was empty of inhabitants but standing; another report says its walls had collapsed over its roofs, and على may mean “with” its buildings.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي. ساقطة متهدمة جدرانها على سقوفها بعد سقوط السقوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The circumstantial clause may modify the passerby or the village; treating it as a delayed adjective of the indefinite village is less likely because of the wāw. The preposition attaches to an implied “settled” if empty, or to “collapsed” if ruinous.
rows.anchor: وهذه الجملة في موضع الحال من الفاعل الذي في: مر، أو: من قرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One historical account says Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Jerusalem after Israel’s wrongdoing, and Jeremiah or Uzayr stood by the great mound created from the city’s soil.
rows.anchor: قيل: لما خرب بخت نصر البابلي بيت المقدس، حين أحدثت بنو إسرائيل الأحداث

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari regards the passerby as an unbeliever in resurrection, suggested by the sequence after Nimrod and the question “how”; another view says Uzayr or Khidr sought firsthand reassurance like Abraham.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: والمار كان كافرا بالبعث وهو الظاهر لانتظامه مع نمروذ

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali argues the passerby cannot be a prophet because prophets do not doubt in this way.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي: لا يجوز أن يكون نبيا لأن مثل هذا الشك لا يقع للأنبياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Life and death may be metaphorical for a city’s rebuilding and ruin, or literal for its inhabitants; the literal reading requires an implied “people” or a reference to their decayed remains.
rows.anchor: والإحياء والإماتة هنا مجازان، عبر بالإحياء عن العمارة، وبالموت عن الخراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the metaphorical reading, the question laments the ruined city of his loved ones and prompts reflection; on the literal reading it recognizes the inability to know how resurrection works while magnifying God, not doubting His power.
rows.anchor: فعلى القول بالمجاز يكون قوله: أنى يحيي على سبيل التلهف من الواقف

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari cites an interpretation that the question was doubt in God’s power, which explains why the man received a personal demonstration.
rows.anchor: وحكى الطبري عن بعضهم أنه قال: كان هذا القول شكا في قدرة الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God caused the man to live again, with movement and the ability to travel.
rows.anchor: فأماته الله مائة عام ثم بعثه أي أحياه وجعل له الحركة والانتقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says after seventy years God protected the dead man from animals and sight, directed Persian king Lusak to rebuild Jerusalem with thousands of foremen and workers, destroyed Nebuchadnezzar with a mosquito, and returned Israelites who rebuilt the city over thirty years.
rows.anchor: قيل: لما مر سبعون سنة من موته، وقد منعه من السباع والطير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The speaker asking how long the man had stayed is apparently God, given the later “how We raise”; alternatives are a heavenly caller, Gabriel, a prophet, or a believer who witnessed the death and lived until the revival. The text does not say God spoke face-to-face.
rows.anchor: قال كم لبثت. الظاهر أن القائل هو الله تعالى لقوله: كيف ننشزها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reasons that the revived man was no longer an unbeliever, so God could address him; Abu Hayyan notes no text says the speech was direct.
rows.anchor: وعلى اختيار الزمخشري لم يكن بعد البعث كافرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “How long?” is a temporal adverbial question asking the duration of his being dead, as a question that elicits acknowledgment.
rows.anchor: و: كم، ظرف، أي: كم مدة لبثت؟ أي: لبثت ميتا

rows.speaker: ابن جريج وقتادة والربيع
rows.claim: They say he died in the morning and revived before sunset a century later, first guessing “a day” before noticing the remaining sun and revising to “part of a day.”
rows.anchor: قال ابن جريج، وقتادة، والربيع: أماته الله غدوة يوم ثم بعثه قبل الغروب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan prefers reading أو as correction rather than uncertainty: once the sun appeared, the man withdrew his mistaken guess and confidently said it was part of a day; “part” can denote most of something.
rows.anchor: والأولى أن لا تكون، أو، هنا للترديد، بل تكون للإضراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A story about Uzayr says he escaped Babylon, reached Heraclius’ monastery by the Tigris, ate fruit and pressed grapes among the empty orchards, then wondered at the ruined village without doubting resurrection; another says his drink was milk.
rows.anchor: في قصة عزير أنه لما نجا من بابل ارتحل على حمار له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says the figs, grapes, and drink remained fresh and unchanged as he left them.
rows.anchor: التين والعنب كما تركه جنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamza and al-Kisaʾi omit the hāʾ in connected recitation as a pause marker; the other seven retain it in connection and pause. The hāʾ is apparently original, though pause-like pronunciation remains possible.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة، والكسائي بحذف الهاء في الوصل على أنها هاء السكت

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy reads “lam yasnah” with assimilation of tāʾ into sīn, as in a similar assimilation elsewhere.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي: لم يسنه، بإدغام التاء في السين

rows.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف وغيره
rows.claim: Talha ibn Musarrif and others read “for one hundred years” instead of “it did not change.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ طلحة بن مصرف وغيره: لمائة سنة، مكان: لم يتسنه

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Abdullah reads “and this is your drink; it did not change.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله: وهذا شرابك لم يتسنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular pronoun in “yatassannah” may refer only to the drink, with a parallel clause about food omitted, or to food and drink jointly treated as one because they are paired or mean sustenance; the negated clause is circumstantial.
rows.anchor: والضمير في: يتسنه مفرد، فيحتمل أن يكون عائدا على الشراب خاصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some grammarians prefer coordinating a clause negated by لم with wāw, while others say لما is preferable; poetic lines illustrate the construction.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعض أصحابنا أن إثبات الواو في الجملة المنفية بلم هو المختار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan says adding wāw to a clause negated by لم is no better than omitting it; both are eloquent and occur in the Qur’an, so the claim that لم is very rare is mistaken.
rows.anchor: وليس إثبات: الواو، مع: لم، أحسن من عدمها، بل يجوز إثباتها وحذفها فصيحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says God revived the man’s eyes first while his body remained dead, then restored him as he watched scattered donkey bones gather and receive flesh; another says the donkey brayed.
rows.anchor: قيل: لما مضت المائة أحيا الله منه عينيه، وسائر جسده ميت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says he watched Jerusalem rebuild while the donkey remained exactly as tied, and the mountain endured a century of wind, rain, sun, and cold; Wahb and al-Dahhak say the donkey remained standing untouched.
rows.anchor: وقيل: رد الله الحياة في عينيه وأخر جسده ميتا، فنظر إلى إيلياء

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari calls the donkey’s survival for a century without food or water one of the greatest signs, like preserving the food and drink.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: وذلك من أعظم الآيات أن يعيشه مائة عام من غير علف ولا ماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “To make you a sign” may have an extra wāw, attach to an implied “we showed you,” or attach to an implied later “we did this”; each links the sign to the revival and preservation.
rows.anchor: ولنجعلك آية للناس قيل: الواو، مقحمة أي: لنجعلك آية

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash says the sign was that the man returned at the same youthful age at which he died while his descendants had become old; Ikrima specifies that he was forty and his sons over a hundred.
rows.anchor: وقال الأعمش: كونه آية هو أنه جاء شابا على حاله يوم مات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations make him a sign because everyone who knew him had died, or because he returned claiming to be Uzayr and recited the Torah from memory without error, prompting people to call him God’s son.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كونه آية هو أنه جاء وقد هلك كل من يعرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan says the Torah had never been recited aloud before Uzayr and that his entire death and return is an enduring sign for people of every age, so no single detail needs to be privileged.
rows.anchor: ولم يقرأ التوراة ظاهرا أحد قبل عزير، فذلك كونه آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The people” may mean his surviving contemporaries or all people through the end of time.
rows.anchor: والألف واللام في: للناس، للعهد إن غنى به من بقي من قومه

rows.speaker: قتادة والضحاك والربيع وابن زيد
rows.claim: These authorities say the bones are his; other views take them as the donkey’s or both. Al-Zamakhshari adds the dead people of the village, which Abu Hayyan rejects because they were not revived there.
rows.anchor: يعني، بالعظام عظام نفسه، قاله قتادة، والضحاك، والربيع، وابن زيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan prefers the donkey’s bones: the command follows the man’s resurrection and dialogue, and “its bones” can be understood by an omitted possessive or by the definite article replacing a pronoun.
rows.anchor: والأظهر أن يراد عظام الحمار، والتقدير: إلى العظام منه

rows.speaker: الحرميان وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: The two Meccan readers and Abu Amr read “nunshiruhā” with ḍamma on nūn and kasra-like rāʾ; Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Abu Haywa, and Aban read it with fatḥa. Both derive from forms meaning revive, though نشر may also evoke unfolding bones after death.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحرميان وأبو عمرو: ننشرها، بضم النون والراء المهملة

rows.speaker: باقي السبعة
rows.claim: The remaining canonical readers use zāy in “nunshizuhā,” meaning move or raise the bones together for reconstruction; other reported vocalizations vary the initial or medial vowels.
rows.anchor: وقرأ باقي السبعة: ننشزها، بضم النون والزاي المعجمة

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy reads “how we create them,” using the verb for creation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي: كيف ننشيها، بالياء أي نخلقها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some argue that bones cannot be alive individually and prefer the zāy reading as joining them; they understand God as raising them from the earth into the body. Abu Hayyan rejects its superiority because the rāʾ reading is mutawātir.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: العظام لا تحيى على الانفراد حتى ينضم بعضها إلى بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects parsing “how we raise them” as a circumstantial clause describing living bones: a full interrogative clause cannot be a circumstantial adjunct, though كيف alone can be.
rows.anchor: وهذا ليس بشيء، لأن الجملة الاستفهامية لا تقع حالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He parses the interrogative clause as an object of the visual verb when it is syntactically suspended by a question, and as a substitute for “the state of the bones”: see their state, how God raises them.
rows.anchor: والذي يقتضيه النظر أن هذه الجملة في موضع البدل من العظام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Suspended interrogatives privilege grammatical form over intended question meaning; Arabic also has constructions where meaning overrides form, and he develops this issue in his grammatical work after a question from Ibn Daqiq al-ʿId about a hadith.
rows.anchor: وليس الاستفهام في باب التعليق مرادا به معناه، بل هذا من المواضع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Clothing” is literally what covers the body and here metaphorically names flesh covering bone; the image is especially apt as a concrete thing covering another concrete thing.
rows.anchor: الكسوة حقيقة هي ما وارى الجسد من الثياب، واستعارها هنا لما أنشأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the man watched flesh, nerves, and veins rejoin; the apparent wording indicates God addressed him after he was fully revived, not while only part of him lived.
rows.anchor: وروي أنه كان يشاهد اللحم والعصب والعروق كيف تلتئم وتتواصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence of commands to look suggests the bones are not the man’s own, unless the verbs for raising and covering stand for having raised and covered them already.
rows.anchor: والتعقيب بالفاء في قوله: فانظر إلى آخره، يدل على أن العظام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each command to inspect the food, drink, and donkey is separated because each is a distinct, powerful miracle; unchanged food and drink are first because perishable things enduring a century are more striking than a living donkey that can forage.
rows.anchor: وتكرر الأمر بالنظر إلى الطعام والشراب في الثلاث الخوارق، ولم ينسق

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet describes a stray camel as able to drink and eat trees until its owner arrives, illustrating why a living animal could survive naturally.
rows.anchor: معها سقاؤها وحذاؤها ترد الماء وتأكل الشجر حتى يأتيها ربها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third look is not an independent sign: it explains what to inspect about the donkey, namely its bones rising and being assembled and clothed with flesh.
rows.anchor: فجاء النظر الثالث توضيحا للنظر الثاني، من أي جهة ينظر إلى الحمار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects the claim that “to make you a sign” is syntactically advanced in wording but delayed in rank; the looks are coordinated in their stated order.
rows.anchor: وليس في الكلام تقديم وتأخير كما زعم بعضهم، وإن الأنظار منسوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This episode is exceptionally strong evidence for resurrection because death and revival were witnessed in this world.
rows.anchor: وفي هذه الآية أقوى دليل على البعث إذ وقعت الإماتة والإحياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers use the active “tabayyana”; Ibn Abbas reads it passive, and Ibn al-Sumayfiʿ reads a passive form without tāʾ. The active verb’s implied subject is the manner of revival that had seemed strange.
rows.anchor: قرأ الجمهور: تبين، مبنيا للفاعل، وقرأ ابن عباس: تبين له، مبنيا للمفعول

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari says the man saw clearly what he had previously thought beyond God’s power; Ibn Atiyya rejects this for imposing the weak interpretation that he doubted resurrection.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري: لما اتضح له عيانا ما كان مستنكرا في قدرة الله

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari supplies an omitted “that God can do everything” as the subject of “became clear,” repeated in the man’s next statement; Abu Hayyan says this is not grammatical “competition” because the two governing verbs do not share a coordinated construction.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري وبدأ به ما نصه: وفاعل تبين مضمر تقديره: فلما تبين له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second clause is governed by “he said,” not “became clear”; the standard cases of shared government involve a conjunction or another genuine relation between the governing expressions.
rows.anchor: فليس العامل الثاني مشتركا بينه وبين: تبين، الذي هو العامل الأول
